question: Where can I find a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer
You can find a fractional CRO through specialized fractional-executive marketplaces like Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, and Bolster, through RevOps and GTM advisory boutiques, through your VC or PE firm's talent network, and through warm referrals from other founders and operators. The fastest reliable path is usually a curated marketplace or a referral, because both pre-vet for real revenue-leadership experience rather than resume keywords.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior go-to-market leader who runs your sales, marketing, and revenue operations on a part-time or contract basis — typically one to three days a week — instead of joining full-time. For companies between roughly $1M and $20M in revenue, that model gives you VP- or C-level revenue horsepower without the $300K-plus base salary, equity grant, and long ramp of a permanent hire. But the market for these people is fragmented and noisy, so knowing *where* to look — and how to filter — matters as much as knowing that you want one.

## What is a fractional CRO and when do you actually need one?
A fractional CRO owns the same mandate as a full-time CRO — revenue predictability, GTM strategy, sales team performance, pipeline health, and cross-functional alignment between marketing, sales, and customer success — but delivers it in a fractional time commitment. The best ones are operators who have already built and scaled revenue orgs, and who now deliberately serve two to four clients at once rather than betting everything on a single company. They tend to arrive with playbooks, hiring networks, and a diagnostic instinct that a first-time VP simply does not have yet.

You typically need one in a few recognizable situations. The founder has been the de facto head of sales and has hit the ceiling of their own time or expertise. Revenue has stalled and nobody can articulate *why* the number is missing. You are about to hire your first sales reps and have no idea how to comp, quota, or coach them. Or you have a board or investor pushing for GTM discipline you cannot yet afford to hire full-time. In each case the fractional model buys you senior judgment during the exact window when a wrong full-time hire would be most expensive. If you want to pressure-test whether the timing is right, our guide on [revenue leadership readiness](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-readiness-signals) walks through the specific signals.

There is also a quieter, less-discussed trigger: the founder who is good at revenue but hates it, or who is being pulled away from product or fundraising by the daily grind of running deals. A fractional CRO is not only a fix for a skills gap; it is a way to reclaim founder time and attention for the work that only the founder can do. Many of the most productive engagements start not because sales is broken, but because the founder has become the single point of failure for every deal over a certain size. When one person is the pipeline, the forecast, the closer, and the sales manager all at once, growth is capped at that person's calendar — and a fractional leader's first job is often simply to make the revenue engine run without the founder physically present in every meeting.

It is worth being honest about when you *don't* need one, too. If you have fewer than a handful of customers and no repeatable motion, no amount of senior revenue leadership will manufacture product-market fit — you likely need the founder still selling directly and learning. If your problem is purely capacity (you need more reps dialing, not better strategy), a fractional CRO is expensive overkill. And if your revenue is genuinely predictable and scaling smoothly, the fractional model may be a bridge you have already crossed and it is time to hire full-time. The model shines in the messy middle: enough traction to be worth optimizing, not enough scale or certainty to justify a permanent C-level bet.

## Where can I find a fractional CRO — the actual channels ranked?
There are five channels worth your time, and they trade off differently on speed, vetting quality, and cost. The map below shows how a typical search flows from need to signed engagement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[You need a fractional CRO] --> B[Referral network]
    A --> C[Fractional marketplaces]
    A --> D[GTM advisory boutiques]
    A --> E[Investor talent networks]
    A --> F[Professional communities]
    B --> G[Shortlist of three to five candidates]
    C --> G
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Working session and reference checks]
    H --> I[Signed engagement]
```

**Referrals from founders and operators** are the highest-signal channel. Ask three or four founders one stage ahead of you who they used and who they would hire again. A referral comes pre-loaded with a real performance track record and honest failure modes, which no marketplace profile gives you. The downside is coverage — you only get the people your network happens to know.

**Curated fractional marketplaces** are the fastest structured option. Platforms such as Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, Bolster, Continuum, and Fractionals United maintain vetted rosters of fractional revenue leaders and can produce a matched shortlist in days rather than weeks. They handle the top-of-funnel filtering for you, and most let you interview several candidates before committing. The tradeoff is that quality varies by platform and you should still run your own references.

**GTM and RevOps advisory boutiques** sit between a single fractional executive and a full agency. Firms like Winning by Design, Skaled, and Revenue Architects place experienced revenue leaders on a fractional or interim basis, often backed by a bench of analysts and playbooks. You pay more, but you get institutional depth and continuity if your fractional leader rotates out.

**Investor talent networks** are underused. If you are venture- or PE-backed, your firm's platform or talent team almost certainly keeps a list of proven fractional CROs they have seen work across the portfolio. That list is effectively a referral filtered through people who have watched these operators perform under real board pressure. For a deeper breakdown of how backers source operators, see our note on [portfolio talent networks](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/investor-talent-networks).

**Professional communities and LinkedIn** round out the list. Communities like Pavilion, RevGenius, and Wizards of Ops are full of practicing and fractional revenue leaders, and LinkedIn's own "Open to fractional work" signals plus targeted search will surface candidates directly. This channel needs the most vetting effort because there is no gatekeeper — but it also has the widest reach and the lowest cost.

A practical note on sequencing these channels: do not run them one at a time. The most efficient search opens two or three in parallel — post the ask to your closest founder network, submit a brief to one curated marketplace, and put out a signal in a community like Pavilion — all in the same week. Running channels in parallel gives you a comparison set, and a comparison set is what protects you from anchoring on the first confident person who happens to be available. A candidate who looks impressive in isolation often looks merely average next to three peers who have run your exact motion. The goal of the search phase is not to find *a* fractional CRO; it is to generate enough real options that you can afford to be selective.

One more channel deserves a mention even though it sits slightly outside the ranked five: fractional CROs frequently refer *each other*. A strong operator who is fully booked, or who recognizes your motion is not their specialty, will often hand you a name of someone who fits better. When you talk to a candidate who passes on the engagement, always ask who they would recommend instead. Those peer referrals are unusually high-signal because they come from someone who understands the work intimately and has no incentive to oversell a colleague they will have to see again at the next community event.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost and how are engagements structured?
Pricing in this market is not standardized, so treat any single number with suspicion and always confirm scope. That said, the common structures are recognizable. Most fractional CROs charge either a **monthly retainer** tied to a fixed number of days per month, an **hourly or daily rate** for lighter advisory work, or a **hybrid** of a smaller retainer plus performance-linked upside. Retainers dominate because both sides want predictability, and because revenue work rarely fits neatly into billable hours.

The variables that move price are seniority, time commitment, industry complexity, and whether the engagement is pure strategy or hands-on execution. A leader spending one day a week advising costs far less than one embedded three days a week actively managing reps and running your forecast. Equity is sometimes part of the package for early-stage companies conserving cash, though many seasoned fractional operators prefer cash given they are diversifying across several clients. Rather than anchor on a specific figure, ask each candidate for their standard structure and what a comparable engagement looked like — the *shape* of their answer tells you how experienced they really are. Our [fractional engagement pricing framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-pricing-models) lays out how to compare offers apples-to-apples.

Contract length usually runs three to twelve months with a clear diagnostic period up front. A strong fractional CRO will insist on a short initial assessment before committing to a longer term, because they want to confirm the problem is one they can actually move. Be wary of anyone who quotes a long fixed engagement before understanding your revenue motion.

When you compare offers, resist the temptation to reduce them to a single monthly number, because the same headline figure can hide very different value. Two candidates might both quote the same retainer, but one is offering pure advisory — a weekly call and a slide deck — while the other is embedding two days a week, sitting in your pipeline reviews, and personally coaching your reps. The second is dramatically more expensive per hour and dramatically more valuable per dollar. The right unit of comparison is not price but price against the specific outcome and time commitment: what will be true about your revenue engine in ninety days, and what will this person actually do to get you there. A candidate who cannot describe their engagement in those terms is selling their calendar, not their expertise.

Watch, too, for how a candidate handles the performance-linked portion of a hybrid deal. Thoughtful operators are usually happy to tie some upside to results they can actually influence — pipeline created, a fixed rebuild of the comp plan, a repeatable forecast process stood up — but they will push back hard on being paid on a top-line revenue number they do not fully control, especially in a long sales cycle where deals they seeded may close months after they have rotated out. That pushback is a good sign. It means they understand the difference between influence and attribution, which is exactly the discipline you are hiring them to bring to your own revenue reporting.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire the wrong one?
Vetting is where most searches go wrong, because a polished LinkedIn and a confident pitch are easy to fake and hard to verify under time pressure. Build your evaluation around evidence of outcomes, fit with your specific motion, and references who watched them operate. The flow below shows a disciplined evaluation sequence.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Candidate shortlist] --> B[Screen for motion fit]
    B --> C[Ask for concrete outcome stories]
    C --> D[Run a paid working session]
    D --> E[Check three references]
    E --> F{Evidence of real impact}
    F -->|Yes| G[Offer engagement]
    F -->|No| H[Pass and continue search]
```

**Screen for motion fit first.** A fractional CRO who scaled a product-led, self-serve SaaS business may be the wrong fit for a founder-led enterprise deal with six-month sales cycles. Ask specifically about the deal sizes, sales motions, and customer segments they have actually operated in, not just the logos on their profile.

**Demand concrete outcome stories.** The strongest signal is a specific, numbers-backed narrative: what the revenue problem was, what they changed, and what happened to pipeline, win rate, or ramp time as a result. Vague claims about "driving growth" are a red flag. Push for the *mechanism* — how they diagnosed it and what levers they pulled.

**Run a short paid working session.** Before signing a multi-month engagement, pay for a focused diagnostic — a pipeline review, a forecast audit, or a comp-plan critique. You learn more from two hours of real work than from five interviews, and a confident fractional operator will welcome it. Watch whether they ask sharp questions and whether their recommendations are specific to your business or recycled boilerplate.

**Check three references, and ask the hard question.** Speak to at least one founder who kept them and one who did not renew. The single most useful question is: "Would you hire them again, and for what specifically would you *not* use them?" Honest references name limits. If every reference is uniformly glowing, dig harder. For a full vetting checklist, see [how to evaluate a fractional revenue leader](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/vet-fractional-cro).

Beyond those four steps, pay attention to how a candidate talks about *your* problem versus their past wins. Weaker operators steer every conversation back to their greatest hits, because their playbook is a fixed template they apply everywhere. Stronger ones spend most of the conversation asking about your motion, your data, and your team — because they know their diagnosis has to precede their prescription. In the working session especially, notice whether their recommendations change once they see your actual numbers. If the plan they pitch you before looking at your pipeline is identical to the plan they give after, they are not diagnosing; they are dispensing. The whole value of a fractional CRO over a generic consultant is judgment applied to specifics, and specifics are only visible once they get their hands on your real data.

Finally, vet for the exit as deliberately as you vet for the engagement. A good fractional CRO is building something that can outlast them — documented process, a hire-able org design, a forecast the founder can run alone — not making themselves permanently indispensable. Ask directly in the interview what "done" looks like and how they will hand off. Operators who describe a clear off-ramp, including the moment they recommend converting to a full-time hire or tapering to light advisory, are aligned with your long-term interest. Ones who cannot describe how the engagement ends may be optimizing for their own retainer rather than your independence, and that misalignment tends to surface exactly when the work is going well and it is time to let go.

## What is the difference between a fractional CRO, an interim CRO, and a consultant?
These titles get used interchangeably and they are not the same, which matters because you will search different channels depending on which you actually need. A **fractional CRO** is an ongoing, part-time member of your leadership team — they carry the revenue mandate continuously but at reduced hours, and the relationship is meant to persist for months or longer. An **interim CRO** is a full-time placeholder filling a gap, usually while you search for a permanent hire or navigate a transition; the commitment is heavier but explicitly temporary. A **consultant or advisor** delivers recommendations and frameworks but does not own the number or manage the team — they hand you a plan and leave execution to you.

The practical implication is about ownership and accountability. If your revenue is missing and you need someone to *run* the org and be accountable for the result, you want fractional or interim leadership, not advisory. If you have a capable team but need strategic direction or a specific playbook, a consultant may be enough and cheaper. Many of the marketplaces and boutiques listed above staff all three models, so be explicit in your outreach about which you want — otherwise you will get mismatched candidates. Our comparison of [fractional versus interim versus advisory](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-interim-advisory) breaks down when each fits.

One more distinction worth flagging: a fractional CRO is not the same as a sales agency or an outsourced SDR shop. Those provide capacity — bodies making calls — while a fractional CRO provides *leadership* — strategy, hiring, process, and accountability. Confusing the two is a common and costly mistake for founders who think they are buying strategy and actually bought call volume.

The accountability difference shows up most sharply in how each role relates to your team. A fractional CRO typically holds real authority over your sellers — they set quotas, run the forecast call, coach reps directly, and sometimes make hiring and firing recommendations that stick. An interim CRO holds even more, because they are the full-time seat until a permanent leader arrives, and the team reports to them without ambiguity. A consultant, by contrast, has no line authority at all; they influence through persuasion and hand their conclusions back to you to enforce. This is why a brilliant consulting deck so often fails to change anything: the person who wrote it has no mandate to make the org do it. If your core problem is that good ideas are not getting executed, buying more ideas will not help — you need someone with the standing to drive change through the team, and that means fractional or interim leadership, not advisory.

Choosing correctly also affects cost and speed of impact. Advisory is the cheapest and the slowest to move the number, because execution stays on your plate. Interim is the most expensive and the fastest to stabilize a crisis, because you are effectively renting a full-time executive at premium rates. Fractional sits deliberately in the middle — enough embedded ownership to change outcomes, at a fraction of the full-time cost, for situations that are serious but not emergencies. Naming which of the three you actually need, in plain language, before you start reaching out is one of the highest-leverage things you can do to shorten the search and avoid interviewing a stack of people who were never going to fit.

## Related questions
### How is a fractional CRO different from a VP of Sales?
A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue engine — marketing, sales, and customer success alignment plus forecasting — while a VP of Sales owns execution within the sales function specifically. The CRO operates a level up, on strategy and cross-functional revenue architecture.

### Can an early-stage startup afford a fractional CRO?
Often yes, precisely because the model is designed for it. Paying for one to two days a week of senior revenue leadership costs a fraction of a full-time C-level hire, letting pre-Series-B companies access experience they otherwise could not fund.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run three to twelve months, opening with a short diagnostic period. The relationship often evolves — some convert to a permanent hire, others taper to light advisory once the revenue org is stable and self-sufficient.

### Should my fractional CRO take equity instead of cash?
It depends on your cash position and their preference. Early-stage companies conserving runway sometimes blend a smaller retainer with equity, but many experienced fractional operators prefer cash because they diversify across multiple clients.

### Where do fractional CROs usually come from?
Most are former full-time VPs of Sales, CROs, or GTM leaders who scaled revenue orgs and now deliberately serve several companies at once. The best have a track record of building repeatable revenue systems, not just closing deals.

## FAQ
**What does a fractional CRO actually do day to day?**
They diagnose revenue problems, set GTM strategy, build or fix sales processes and comp plans, coach and sometimes hire sales leaders, run or overhaul the forecast, and align marketing, sales, and customer success. The specific mix depends on where your revenue engine is breaking.

**How quickly can I hire a fractional CRO?**
Through a curated marketplace or a strong referral, you can have a shortlist within days and a signed engagement within two to four weeks. Cold-sourcing through LinkedIn or communities takes longer because you carry the full vetting load yourself.

**What size company hires a fractional CRO?**
Most commonly companies between roughly $1M and $20M in revenue — past the earliest scrappy stage but not yet able or ready to justify a full-time CRO. That said, larger companies also use them for interim coverage or specific turnaround projects.

**Is a fractional CRO worth it versus hiring full-time?**
When you need senior revenue judgment but cannot yet justify a permanent C-level salary and equity grant, yes. The model also de-risks the decision — you get experienced leadership now and can convert to full-time later once you know the role and the person.

**How do I write a scope of work for a fractional CRO?**
Define the specific revenue outcome you want, the time commitment, the decision authority they hold, the systems and team they will touch, and the review cadence. A clear scope is the single best predictor of a successful engagement — vague scopes produce vague results.

**Can a fractional CRO manage my existing sales team?**
Yes, and many engagements center on exactly that — coaching reps, restructuring quotas and territories, and installing management rhythm. Confirm up front how much direct people-management authority they will have, because leading a team fractionally requires clear mandate from the founder.

**What are red flags when choosing a fractional CRO?**
Vague outcome stories with no numbers, a refusal to do a paid working session, uniformly glowing references with no stated limits, a motion mismatch with your business, and pressure to sign a long engagement before any diagnostic. Any one of these warrants a harder look.

**Do fractional CROs sign non-competes given they work with multiple clients?**
They rarely sign broad non-competes because serving several clients is the model, but they should sign confidentiality agreements and disclose any direct competitive conflicts. Ask directly whether they currently work with any competitor before engaging.

**How do I measure whether a fractional CRO is working?**
Set two or three leading indicators at the start — pipeline created, forecast accuracy, ramp time, or win rate on a defined segment — and review them on a fixed cadence. Leading indicators move within a quarter; revenue itself may lag the engagement, so judging solely on the top-line number too early is misleading.

**Can a fractional CRO convert to a full-time hire later?**
Frequently, and many founders treat the engagement as an extended try-before-you-buy. Discuss the possibility openly at the outset, including how the equity and compensation would change, so a future conversion feels like a natural next step rather than an awkward renegotiation.
